whisper_segs.text: Good morning.
It's 7 o'clock on Thursday the 5th of March.
This is Morning Ireland on RTE Radio 1 with Sarah McInerney and Gavin Jennings.
On today's programme, another missile barrage from Iran as the US Senate backs Trump's war powers.
A flight from Dubai touches down in Dublin.
One in ten request a right to remote working and a plume of dust is on its way from the Sahara.
In business annual results from PTSB, we'll hear from its CEO and China forecasts its slowest growth in 35 years.
And coming up in sport, Arsenal win and City draw.
It sees the Gunners go seven points clear at the top of the Premier League.
Well, with you till nine, the news is read by Karen Carty.
The first commercial flight to bring citizens home from Dubai to Ireland since last Saturday arrived in Dublin Airport late last night.
Another Emirates flight is scheduled to leave Dubai this afternoon and is due to land in Dublin this evening.
Cathy Lee reports.

There were emotional scenes at Dublin Airport last night as 384 passengers arrived to Ireland after being stuck in Dubai since the war caused severe travel disruption to airline traffic across the Middle East.
The first commercial flight, Emirates Flight EK163, landed at Dublin Airport at 11 o'clock.
Some of the passengers were transiting through Dublin before going on to other European destinations, while others were coming home from other parts of the world, having transited through Dubai.
Family members waiting for their loved ones said the last few days had been a worrying time waiting for news of flights.
More commercial flights are to follow today, but the first government-chartered flight from Oman is due later this week.
The Minister for Foreign Affairs, Helen McEntee, has said she expects the government to charter more flights if necessary to bring Irish citizens stranded in the Middle East home.
US politicians have voted against a war powers measure that would have limited Donald Trump's ability to order further military action in Iran.
Senators voted almost entirely down party lines.
Our Washington correspondent, Jackie Fox.
This was the first test of Congress's support for Operation Epic Fury.
Democrats have argued that Donald Trump
Trump did not have the authority to launch it.
Congress is the only branch of government that can officially declare war.
Last night, the Republican-held Senate voted on whether to limit President Trump's ability to order further strikes against Iran.
It failed in a 47-53 vote, mostly along party lines.
The House is set to vote on a similar resolution today.
Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson said he believed he has the votes to defeat it.
Jackie Fox, RT News, Washington.
Iran launched missiles at Israel overnight as aerial attacks in the Middle East continued for a sixth day.
The US and Israel have intensified their bombing of Iran, with Israel's military also targeting Beirut's southern suburbs.
Kate Varley from our Foreign Desk reports.
Fresh explosions have been reported in Iran's capital Tehran and the nearby city of Karaj this morning, after Israel's military said it had begun a new wave of widespread strikes.
Air raid sirens were also heard in Israel, with missiles intercepted by air defences above Tel Aviv and Jerusalem overnight,
while in Lebanon, an Israeli airstrike reportedly hit a Hezbollah stronghold in South Beirut this morning.
As the war enters its sixth day, the UN has warned that the continuing violence is triggering mass displacement.
Around 100,000 people left Tehran in the first...
two days following the attacks, while in Lebanon, around 80,000 people have been forced to leave their homes, according to local authorities.
A code of practice for the right to request remote working is to be strengthened as part of a review by the government.

The Department of Enterprise is to recommend that the Workplace Relations Commission revises the code to ensure employers give comprehensive and transparent reasons for their remote working decisions.
Our work and technology correspondent Brian O'Donovan reports.
As part of this review of the right to request remote work, the government undertook a public consultation as well as surveys of employers and employees.

There was a strong perception among workers that the legislation is a toothless tiger weighted in favour of the employer who can refuse remote working requests on business grounds without going into the details of why the request was denied.
The Workplace Relations Commission is to be asked to strengthen its code of practice to support more detailed and transparent reasons from employers for refusing remote work.
The review also found that less than half of employees in Ireland are aware of the right to request remote work.
In a bid to address this, the Department of Enterprise is to launch a targeted national information campaign to increase knowledge and understanding of the legislation.
Poultry has been culled at a premises in County Tyrone following a suspected outbreak of bird flu.
Northern Ireland's chief vet said he'd taken the decision to impose restrictions
restrictions in the area of the premises near Newton Stewart.
The move is based on clinical signs at the facility and preliminary test results.
A temporary control zone has been established around the business.
Repair works have been completed at Dundalk's Oriole Park after the newly installed AstroTurf pitch was damaged by flares.
The incident happened during a recent fixture between Dundalk FC and Drogheda United.
Both clubs condemned the incident and Drogheda United said it would cover the full cost of the damage.
The club was also fined €15,000 by the League of Ireland's Disciplinary Committee.
And now the weather.
RTE Radio and Weather with Grant.
Future-proof your home and comfort with the HVO Biofuel Ready Grant Vortex Condensing Boiler.
Think heating, think Grant.
Visit grant.ie.

A cool day with highest afternoon temperatures of 3 to 8 degrees.

Celebrating selling more electric cars in January than any other car brand.
At Hyundai dealerships nationwide.
With the latest traffic and travel news, I'm Sinead Newloughan.
To Meath first, as there's a collision on the M3 southbound.

And in Cork, slow now on the Wilton Road northbound at Dennehy's Cross.
That's the latest traffic and travel news.
Sinead, thank you very much for that.
Now, John S.
Doyle joins us with a look at what it says in today's papers.
The charge of €800 per adult for a charter flight from the Gulf War Zone, organised by the Irish government for Irish citizens, is a shakedown.
That's the view of the Social Democrats'Senator Patricia Stevenson, quoted in the Irish Independence League story.
The Department of Foreign Affairs has said it is bearing a portion of the cost of tomorrow's flight from Oman, aimed at getting vulnerable citizens home as a priority.
And a spokesman said that details of the costs would be available after the repatriations were completed.
The Irish Times highlights the fact that the US-Israel war on Iran has spread to the Indian Ocean.
That's after a US submarine torpedoed an Iranian frigate off Sri Lanka, killing at least 87 people.
And NATO air defences shot down an Iranian ballistic missile headed for Turkey.
On the fifth day of the war, the U.S.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the joint U.S.-Israeli military campaign has dealt sheer destruction for our radical Islamist Iranian adversaries.
In a new form of diplomatic language, he said, they are toast.
They know it, or they will know it soon enough.
That phrase gives the Irish Sun its lead headline.
The Irish Examiner reports that as concerns grow about energy costs here because of the war, the government has ruled out the reintroduction of energy credits and excise cuts on fuel.
And the war has caused chaos in the fertilizer trade, according to the Irish Farmers'Journal.
Rachel Donovan reports that supply and price of urea-based products is a real concern among importers, some of which pulled price lists and existing quotations on Wednesday.
In other stories, the Irish Daily Mail leads with a report that property developers are paying for an event in the frame.
Riviera City of Cannes that will be attended by the Department of Housing to court institutional investors.
Craig Hughes writes that internal documents show that officials expect costs of €300,000 for next week's event to be covered by what are described as private market sponsors.
The department is quoted as saying that such funding of their participation at the event was in line with other countries.

The parents of a 14-year-old girl, Leona Harper, killed in the explosion in Cressla, County Donegal, four years ago, say they are hurt by the refusal of the Minister for Justice, Jim O'Callaghan, to meet them.
The minister, for his part, said he did not wish to jeopardise the advanced Garda investigation.
He said earlier this week, I want the Cressla families to get justice, and the only place that justice comes is in the...
courts.
In the courts also are the Burke family of Castle Bar, or some of them.

The papers note that Martina Burke and her daughter Ami were not in court yesterday to hear Judge Brian Cregan sentence them to two weeks in prison for contempt of court in relation to the case of their respectively son and brother,
Enoch.
The judge said it was long past time for the court to call a halt to this family circus.
It's the lead story for the Irish Daily Star under the headline, Send in the Clowns.
John Estoyle, it's ten past seven.
We'll hear from people on that flight home from Dubai last night next.
Morning Ireland, 11 minutes past 7, war in Iran, day 6.
The first direct flight to Dublin Airport from the Middle East since the US and Israel started their bombing campaign and Iran retaliated, arrived home last night.
384 people were on board the Emirates flight from Dubai, which touched down just before 11pm.
Another Emirates flight is scheduled to leave Dubai at 5 past 2 local time and due to land here just before 7 o'clock this evening.
Our reporter Andrew Louth was in Dublin Airport yesterday where families were reunited.
Narita Geary from Newcastle West in County Limerick arriving home last night.
It's just so good to be home.
It was unreal.
It was very unreal.
I mean, you see these things on television, you see them in movies, but you just don't think you'll end up there yourself.
You know, you're coming home from a holiday.
We got home.
Woo!
She was one of 384 passengers to arrive to Dublin direct from Dubai on board Emirates flight EK163.
Kevin Murphy from Dublin was waiting for his wife Gina Quinn to walk through the doors at arrivals.
She was woken, I think, three or four times during the night.
The authorities sent out text alerts.
And they're quite alarming, the sound they make on your phone, and they all said, incoming missiles detected, shelter in place, keep away from windows.
Her approach was to have a bag of clothes ready at the hotel door, just to be able to scoot out.
After that, it calmed down a bit, but there was always that uncertainty, would a missile come from someplace?
Right up to take-off today, you know, we were all watching it on flight radar today.
When Gina arrived, she was relieved, as was Kevin.
It was pretty awful for the first 24 hours because you just didn't know what was happening and there was a lot of noises.
A national alarm in the middle of...
the night that woke us all up on our mobile phones.
So it was very frightening.
I have to say the airlines were great, but they were inundated.
So I think everybody on the flight coming in tonight is really delighted and I just hope that everybody else gets home quickly.
Kevin, now that Gina's home, how do you feel?
Delighted, absolutely delighted.
You know, we can relax now.
I mean, I hope everybody else who's out there gets home safely too.
It's just a lovely feeling.
Jennifer Hodgins was welcomed by her mother and sister.
Saturday was probably the worst of it, Saturday night.
It would be kind of quiet every now and then during the day and a few drones or a few bits kind of in the sky, but they looked after us very well, to be fair, and we felt safe enough during the day.
It was just night time was probably the scary part, really.
Did you find yourselves getting calmer as the days went on or was there concern that you still were there and you didn't seem to be getting out anytime soon?
Yeah, I think just with the cancellations, you were constantly being updated that you were on a flight and then it was cancelled that night.
I guess you were just getting frustrated or anything.
No one could do anything about it.
Yeah, it was just a bit scary as the days went on that you weren't getting home.
A weight lifted off your shoulders then?
Yeah, definitely.
It's nice to be back now on Irish soil anyway.
While excitement, tears, joy and relief was order of the night, some were frustrated.
with how messaging was communicated.
Cormac Ferguson and Aoife Gath from County Meath were among them.
The not knowing, kind of left in limbo, was kind of the biggest frustration about everything.
You know, we didn't know where we were coming or going.
Yeah, not being able to talk to Emirates at all.
Like, we only got to speak to Emirates.
Was it today?
This morning?
Yeah.
Yeah, so it was four days before we could actually speak to somebody in Emirates.
We never got any email or anything, so we were just waiting constantly to hear from them, but we were never going to hear from them.
When we eventually spoke to somebody today, they said, we're not going to be able to contact everyone, so it's your responsibility to contact us.
As a whole, it's been lacklustre response, like government-wise, embassy.
Emirates, it just hasn't been good enough.
Like, loads of people are left in limbo.
The only reason we're on that flight is because we were ignorant enough.
We went to the airport.
We were told not to go to the airport.
We've seen there was a flight going today at half five.
If we hadn't gone to the airport, we wouldn't be on that flight.
There's plenty of people on that flight that aren't actually going to Dublin as their last destination.
They just took the first flight they could.
And the confusion that's been caused as well.
The minister put out that there was a flight coming home today by Emirates.
It wasn't publicised by Emirates on their website that there was a flight going home.
While for Monica Miller and her daughter Susan from County Leash, they were just happy to be home.
We were terrified we were going to be separated or we didn't know, you know, because they just had vague names.
Yeah, they had a room number from the hotel.
So once we knew we'd all boarding cards, we got through security, got through passport control, we knew we were in the airport then ready for a deploring fight.
So when you were watching the map on the plane,
Just when we got as far as Greece, was it right?
Exactly.
When we knew we were flying over Europe, we knew we were well away from anything that we'd left behind.
So, yeah, thrilled.
We just feel sorry for some people we met in the hotel that are still out there waiting.
So we're just keeping our fingers crossed that they get the flight tomorrow to come home as well.
Because, you know, still a lot of people out there.
That's Monica and Susan Miller from County Leash ending that report from Andrew Louth.
It's 17 minutes past seven.

Well, as Irish people make their way home, Iran launched a new barrage of missiles towards Israel last night, while US lawmakers voted against a war powers measure that would have limited Donald Trump's ability to order further military action in Iran.
AFP spoke to a number of Iranians who fled the country in Turkey through the Capicoy border.
I'm coming from Tehran and there is a lot of chaos in the city, a lot of missiles and attacks from US and Israel.
I'm not into their politics but I know it's a lot of...
It brings just a lot of sadness to people.
We hear some things, some pollutions outside of the city, but not inside of the city.
Sleeping in fear and waking up in stress.
So situation is a little bit awful.
The future?
I think because Iran has so much...
And I think this war, it's finished very soon.
And I think after one, peace is coming for our people.
Well, for the latest on developments overnight, we go now to Tel Aviv and Sikundra Kermani, who's Channel 4 News foreign correspondent.
And Sikundra, thank you for joining us.
Can you talk us through, firstly, what happened overnight?
Good to be with you.
Yes, overnight we had three or four alerts of incoming missiles from Iran.
That comes after a number of nights where we had no such alerts.
All of those largely were intercepted, no fatalities reported overnight.
Of course, Israel's air defences are generally quite strong.
We have seen on a few occasions missiles penetrate through, though.
The Israeli authorities are saying that the rate of fire of ballistic missiles from Iran towards Israel has significantly slowed over recent days.
And as a result, they're looking at somewhat easing restrictions on public life later today from...
Essential activities only to limited activities.
I think Iran's military capacity to launch missiles and drones has been seriously degraded by these very powerful Israeli and American strikes on it.
Iran is also likely deliberately trying to conserve
some of its supplies in order to try and prolong the conflict as much as possible.
It's also quite clear that the Gulf Arab states are, for Iran right now, at least as much of a target as Israel is, if not more so, because the attacks that Iran has been able to launch
on the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, etc., have had, in many ways, a greater global impact, disrupting the crucial oil and gas industries there, causing chaos in terms of travel disruption too.
And I think that's all part of it.
Deliberate strategy by Iran to try and raise the global cost of this conflict, hoping that that in turn will lead President Trump to end the war sooner rather than later.
There's no sign of that happening at the moment.
Indeed, a significant development in the US as well overnight, where the Senate rejected a motion that was aimed at reining in Donald Trump's power to order further military action.
So would you expect that means now the US administration can do what it wants?
And if so, what does it want?
Yeah, that's a good question.
Where does it go and how does this end?
I mean, in some ways, given the level of destruction to Iran's military capacities, as well as, of course,
it seems the deaths of hundreds of Iranian civilians, then it's hard to know exactly at what stage President Trump wants to stop.
He could stop at any time because he could say we have achieved our goals of massively degrading Iran's nuclear or ballistic missile capacities.
The Americans seem to be talking less about regime change than they were at the very outset of the war at the moment.
Last night, there were kind of repeated reports that turned out eventually to be wrong, that Iranian Kurdish rebel groups based across the border in Iraq were beginning a ground offensive
against the regime with the backing of the CIA and the Mossad.
Now, as I said, those reports turned out to be false.
At the same time, those rebel groups, you know, it seems still quite possible that they may launch some kind of attacks against regime forces in the west of the country in the coming days.
And that may well be the new phase of the conflict.

Of course, many analysts have pointed out it's very difficult to try and topple a regime or even bring it to its knees just by air power alone or done in some kind of conjunction with some kind of ground force.
And the Kurds are perhaps the ones best suited to that.
Although many analysts also pointing out that this is a recipe for really for civil war and potential absolute chaos in the country and warning against it.
Yeah, and just on that point that you're mentioning, just coming in on the wires, Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they hit Kurdish bases in Iraqi Kurdistan region with three missiles.
That's coming from state media and that's just coming through at the moment, Sekunder.
In terms of the objectives, can I bring you back to that for a second?
Because as you say, it's not entirely clear what the US objective was.
They were talking about regime change.
They're talking about that less now.
Do the US objectives align with the Israeli objectives?
Because I saw a very interesting quote from Danny Citrinovich, who is the former head of the Iran division in the IDF.
He was quoted in the Financial Times yesterday and he said, if we can have a coup, great.
If we can have people on the streets, great.
If we can have a civil war, great.
Israel couldn't care less about the future or stability of Iran.
We want to ensure Iran stays in disarray.
Is that what Israel wants, do you think?
Well, I think Israel certainly wants the Iranian regime to be severely weakened.
There's no secret that the Israeli state wants the regime toppled, if that's toppled.
And, you know, I think Danny Citrinovich was there summarizing what he assessed the Israeli position to be.
And it's accurate.
I don't think that...
that the Israelis are worried about the prospect of civil war in Iran, because that means that there's chaos in Iran, and Iran, as they perceive it, doesn't pose any kind of threat to them.
Whereas other countries in the region, the Arab countries, as a result, perhaps America too, have a greater interest in not seeing huge levels
of chaos, which emanate out in terms of then refugee flows, potential, you know, other neighboring countries also getting involved or becoming destabilized, extremist groups potentially
playing a greater role or some kind of, you know, insurgency by remnants of the regime against any new government that's forming there.
The Israelis probably feel that they're insulated from that and that that is something that they can live with.
That may well prove to be, you know, a very short-termist strategy, if that is their thinking.
But I think also from, you know, the Israeli and American perspective, where they're probably on the same pages, that in some ways, whatever happens.
At this stage, they can live with because of the level of damage that they're doing to Iran's regime.
What the regime is trying to do, I think, is simply ensure its survival.
All it wants to do is just stay fighting.
back on making any kind of massive concessions that appear to be tantamount to a capitulation.
And then at the end, if they're still there, no matter how weak they are, they can declare it a victory themselves.
Very interesting, Sukhendra.
And thank you for joining us.
That's Sukhendra Kermani there, who's Channel 4 News foreign correspondent.
And we'll be hearing from a former CIA analyst a little later in the programme about Israel's or Iran's chance of surviving.
Now back home and after all that rain, some very welcome sunshine this week.
There's a lovely picture in the Irish Times of people sitting out in Stephen's Green in Dublin yesterday afternoon.
Unthinkable this year before now.
If your mind and plans are already drifting to the sea and saying hello to the creatures that live there, a new plan this morning
for how to get familiar and protect the whales, porpoises and puffins and more who live off the coast of Cork and Kerry and draw lots of people there to take a look.
Our environment correspondent George Lee is here.
A plan then, George, a voluntary code.
Tell us more.

Well, it's become big business, particularly, we remember we had Fungi the dolphin, who kept people very amused and entertained and so on down in the Dingle Bay area for maybe 35 years or there, and then suddenly disappeared.
And throughout that time, a new industry really grew up, I suppose, in Ireland, which was a safari, marine safaris, going out on boats to see some of these animals.
And Fungi kept people very busy in Dingle Bay, but there were much, much more.
And so now it's become a big business.
And more and more people, when they go to coastal areas, they like the idea of...
having a tour to do, and so both operators are bringing people out to see a lot of these creatures.
The thing is, in doing that, it's become, there are no rules and regulations, and yet an awful lot of disturbance can happen.
And so, you know, how, for instance, you might approach some of these animals, would you cut too close, would there be too many boats, would there be too much noise, those kind of things.
So it's a question of putting the rules and regulations in place, and that's what this is about.
What sort of animals are we talking about here?
Oh, there's so many.
I mean, in Irish waters in recent years, you have the humpback whale, which seemingly that there have been very many of them in some years.
There's the basking shark, which there used to be a lot of basking sharks in UK waters and around the Isle of Man and in Scotland.
They're diminished now in recent years, but they're turning up around the southwest coast of Ireland quite a lot.
And people really like to see those big creatures.
You're looking at things like lots of seals.
Did you know that we have, I think, half of the world's populations of grey seal are in Irish and British waters?
And they were protected since 1914.
They were one of the first protected mammals out there in the sea.
And so, again, protecting them.
So people come along and they disturb them and off they go and they scatter.
There's a lot of seabirds.
The gannet, which comes, and there's quite a lot of them.
And they would, I mean, they dive for mackerel.
They dive for other pelagic fish.
They have wingspans of two metres.
And they can dive at a rate of nearly 100 kilometres per hour.
People go out to see all of these.
And dolphins, obviously, loads of dolphins.
Turtles.
There's about five or six different varieties of turtles in Irish water.
There's loads to see.
And the more that people go out and turn their attention to what's there, the more interesting it becomes.
So in terms of the impact already visible from disturbances caused by human activity, what are we seeing?
We're seeing potential disturbance, a lot of disturbance is potential because some of these animals or some of these creatures would be put off by, say, noise.
You've got whales who use sound for hunting.
And so the noise of a lot of the boats which might come if they're very noisy, that would cause them to scatter.
We've seen lots of various species who have disappeared.
There were 200 Greenland white-fronted geese out there for a number of years.
They're gone.
Arctic terns don't come anymore.
So there's stuff like that.
So we can scare them off.
So this code, it's been drawn up by people who are involved in the industry in terms of bringing people out there and also people involved in protecting them.
You've been speaking to some of those people.
I have indeed.
William Hunt is the District Conservation Officer of the National Parks and Wildlife Service.
He said this.
The waters off the southwest are highly productive.
They come here to feed on that productivity, whether it's small fish or plankton.
They also come here in terms of the seabirds to breed.
Those seabirds are true seabirds.
They spend all of their lives at sea except for when they come ashore.
And they come ashore down here because they have shelter and they have good feeding opportunities.
So they can raise their young for the six to eight weeks that they spend on the cliffs and islands off the southwest and then head back offshore again.
So they're...
You know, we have...
some numbers of population that account for up to 10% of the global population for things like European storm petrels.

So it's vitally important down here that we protect them and respect them and give them the space they need to do that, while also respecting local communities'ability to bring people out to share in that wildlife spectacle and to support the...
Sustainability of those local communities.
That's William Hunt from the National Parks and Wildlife Service.
Who else were you talking to, George?
I was also talking with Mick Sheeran.
Mick Sheeran operates the Blasket Islands Eco-Marine Tours and he's been in and around the Blasket Islands for over 50 years.
He's seen lots of species come and go and he sees the business particularly growing.
In fact, he was saying that for many years the guys in Ingle Bay, they kept going, looking at Fungi the dolphin and he had the whole of the Blasket Islands to himself.
And now he says, of course, those fellas are now touring around the Blasket Islands and stuff.
So he had very good insights.
This is Mick Sheeran from the Blasket Island Eco-Marine Tours.
Well, obviously, humpback whales with the big one.
Basking shark, when I was fishing there years ago, you'd see a nod basking shark maybe in the start of May.
Then of course with the salmon fishing, basically there was a period there 12, 15 years, never saw a basking shark.
And I thought I never would see a basking shark again.
And they gradually came back.
And now some years we might have a couple of hundred in a day at the start of the season here.
The same with humpback whales.
I never saw a humpback whale when I was fishing.
And then about the year 2005 or so, when we started doing the tours around the island and going further out looking at wildlife,
we started spotting humpback whales and they became very, very plentiful.
I mean, there was one year there we had a humpback whale every day in August.
That's Mick Sheeran from Blasket Islands Eco-Marine Tours from Ventry near Dingle ending that report from George.
We hope the whales like rain because there's a lot of it on the way today.

So that's done.
You also have a continuous outcry on an ongoing basis about why isn't this game on, why isn't that game on, Galway-Roscommon, your own beloved Meade against Cork, etc, etc.
So you have this thing, and I think there needs to be a clear understanding.
going forward among all stakeholders as to what is possible, what is feasible, what are the factors that are at play and what's not possible
and ultimately so that it's clear and people have a clear understanding as to just how much GAA coverage is available because the truth is there's more than ever.
Well, if you're looking for a mature debate, what do you think?
I think Tom Ryan has been very clear about this on an annual basis.
There are four pillars on which the GAA media strategy is based.
Number one is the commercial value of their rights, which is money.
Number two is eyeballs on their games.
Number three is the balance between attendance and coverage.
And number four, then, is the affinity and affection for the Irish language.
So I think when you look at the season and you look at the number of high-profile games, there are going to be clashes and there are going to be games that aren't going to be covered.
But the majority of games are going to be covered.
When I took over the job in RTE, RTE did 40 games a year.
Now we do almost double that.
TG Carher last year did 180.
GAA Plus do 40.
Their predecessor, Sky Sports, did 14.
BBC Northern Ireland do games.
There's more games than ever.
So I think there has to be an understanding that there are more games than ever.
But there has to be a balance as to how many games can be done.
Otherwise, you dilute the games that are at play.
Why?
I mean, if streaming is available, why can't every game be available?
Because I think at that stage, you begin to dilute the games that are available.
You see that in the UK and you've seen it in codes here.
by every game is available.

Of course, but take this week alone.
You can watch Hogan Cup games this week.

There is a multitude.

But there also comes a point whereby you have to protect both the coverage and the attendance that are there.
The attendance is a matter for the GAA.
The coverage is a matter for the broadcasters.
Well, if you're looking for a debate, what are you planning to do with something with the answers that you get to this debate?
I'd love that all the stakeholders would get together and decide what is the best policy.
Because look at the broadcast...
Well, you're one of the stakeholders.
What do you want to do?

A lot of the GAA often don't want games at 1 and 3 on a Saturday.
Provincial towns don't necessarily want because of the traffic congestion, because of shopping onwards.
There are two games on a Sunday, essentially.
On television.
On television, which is where the vast majority of the audience are there.
But there's more to coverage than television.
Yes, absolutely there is.
But at some point, you begin to dilute the coverage.
And I think there needs to be an understanding that's there.
The Friday night option is an option that broadcasters have always claimed for.
There are many who are in favour of it.
The GPA are obviously against it for their own reasons.

But as we've said before, why Meath and Dublin couldn't play on a Friday night or why Armagh and Down couldn't play on the Marshes or the Athletic Grounds on a Friday night and claim that space is another part of the debate that needs to be had.

By the way, separately, because it did come up at the weekend, including in RT's coverage, do you or RT raise any objections with the GAA to Allianz being part of the title of your Sunday night league coverage show?
Because the presenter, Joanne Cantor, said on Saturday night's programme that she had raised a concern back in September.
The team and the production team had asked questions around what was the nature of the contract between the GAA and RTE, and the contract is between the GAA and RTE.
We've been very clear on this.
We honour contracts, and within the contract, the naming rights of the programme are within the GAA contract.
Straightforward.
So had you or RT raised any objections?
Not on the...
No, because it's part of our contract.
So we signed a contract in good faith and we continue to honour that contract.
Do you have any problems with Allianz being associated with the programme?
What problems you may have with Allianz are separate from the contractual arrangement and agreement that you enter into in good faith.
And you respect contracts and you honour contracts.
And the day you start stepping away from contracts, you're in trouble.
Declan, thanks very much for coming in.
It's Declan McBennett, RT's Group Head of Sport.
We'll be talking about flights, getting out and into the Middle East next.

2,000 Irish citizens, many of whom were transiting through Dubai, contacted the Department of Foreign Affairs saying they wanted to leave.

And that is Alison Milton, Ireland's ambassador in the United Arab Emirates.

Good morning, Sarah.

fighter aircraft around, flying with them, those sort of arrangements.
